title: Welcome to Eyrie
author: Emily Foster
summary: Michael Foster introduces the teaching his wife Emily gave at the launch of Eyrie, a new mothers' ministry at their church, arguing that investing in mothers is a way of investing in children and the church's future. Emily Foster's talk opens with the claim that contemporary culture despises children and mothers, then tests that claim against a local Cincinnati moms' Facebook group where a joke about a child preferring cats to children drew an outpouring of approval. She reads such tongue-in-cheek comments as revealing real beliefs and sets them beside fertility data, including a US total fertility rate of 1.60 and a sharp rise in childlessness among women aged 20 to 39. Her move is to concede that motherhood is stressful while insisting that difficulty is precisely what forges fortitude and makes the vocation worthwhile. The second half lays out Eyrie's model: free meetings and childcare, scripture-based instruction, practical homemaking and health skills taught in person, and intergenerational friendship between older and younger mothers. The piece belongs in Family as an argument about motherhood, the home, and how communities support parents.
points: Foster reads a viral local post celebrating a child's wish for cats instead of children as evidence that joking dismissals of motherhood reveal genuine cultural attitudes.
She cites a 45% rise in childlessness since 2006 among women in prime childbearing years and CDC data that nearly 40% of childless women in their 20s do not expect to have children.
Rather than denying that motherhood is stressful, she argues its difficulty is what forges resilience and makes it worthwhile.
Eyrie is deliberately free for both meetings and childcare, contrasting with dues-based moms' groups whose fees flow to a corporate parent.
The ministry prioritizes in-person, intergenerational teaching of practical home skills, on the view that learning beside an experienced mother builds confidence that online tutorials cannot.
quotes: Caring for those who care for the children, building them up, encouraging them, strengthening them, is another way to invest in the spiritual well-being of children.
Tongue-in-cheek statements usually have a core truth, an underlying message that shows what the person actually believes.
It's jarring to hear women speak this way. Motherhood is a gift. A sacred trust. It should be a treasure that we guard, protect, revere and pass down. Not something we belittle, laugh at and mock.

Research from the University of New Hampshire Carsey School shows that out of 44.2 million women in this age tier, 23.1 million have never given birth. This represents a 45% increase in childlessness for this cohort since 2006.

Again, a nugget of truth. Motherhood is not easy. It can be very stressful. But that doesn’t mean it is bad or that we should avoid it simply because it is hard. Often it is the difficulty of a thing that makes it worthwhile.
We want these meetings to give moms a break while also building up and equipping them to do the hard work of mothering. But not in some generic way. Rather in a particular way. In a God-honoring way.
But there is something special about having someone "in the flesh" showing you the ropes. Firstly, the relationship. You don't just "feel" like you know the person. You truly do.
